questions.text: The concept of 'political legitimacy' refers to the
options: Legal right of the government to make and enforce laws
Acceptance and recognition by the people of the government's right to rule
Economic power of the state to control resources
Military strength of the state to enforce its will
questions.explanation: Political legitimacy is the widespread belief that a government has the moral and legal right to exercise authority. It is based on the consent and acceptance of the governed, not merely on legal provisions, economic power, or military force. Without legitimacy, a government may rule through coercion but lacks genuine authority.

questions.text: A major feature of the traditional Igbo political system was the
options: Absence of any form of age-grade organisation
Highly centralised authority of a single monarch
Decentralised nature with governance through village assemblies and councils of elders
Theocratic rule by a priestly class
questions.explanation: The Igbo political system was famously decentralised and acephalous (headless), with decision-making power resting in village assemblies, councils of elders, and age-grade societies. It lacked a centralised monarchy or theocratic rule, which were features of other systems like the Hausa-Fulani or some Yoruba kingdoms.

questions.text: The primary purpose of the Nigerian Constitution is to
options: Serve as a legal document that establishes the framework for governance and protects citizens' rights
Provide a platform for the ruling party to maintain power
Give unlimited powers to the executive branch
Replace all existing customary laws in the country
questions.explanation: A constitution serves as the supreme legal document that establishes the structure of government, defines the powers of its branches, and guarantees fundamental rights to citizens. It is not a tool for a ruling party to maintain power, nor does it grant unlimited executive authority, and it coexists with customary laws.

questions.text: The term 'neo-colonialism' describes the
options: Direct political control of a country by a foreign power
Economic and cultural influence exerted by former colonial powers over independent nations
Military invasion of a country by a neighbouring state
Complete independence of a country from external influence
questions.explanation: Neo-colonialism refers to the indirect control or influence that former colonial powers and other developed nations exert over developing countries through economic dependency, cultural domination, and political manipulation. It is distinct from direct political control (colonialism) or military invasion and represents a form of continued influence after formal independence.

questions.text: A key function of the judiciary in a democratic state is the
options: Interpretation of laws and adjudication of disputes
questions.explanation: The judiciary's primary role is to interpret the law and resolve disputes between individuals, groups, and the state. This includes adjudicating cases and ensuring justice is served. Enforcement of policies is an executive function, budget formulation is a legislative/executive function, and foreign affairs is an executive function.

questions.text: The concept of 'political participation' includes all of the following except
options: Remaining completely indifferent to political issues
questions.explanation: Political participation encompasses all activities by which citizens attempt to influence government decisions, including voting, party membership, and protesting. Indifference or apathy is the absence of participation, not a form of it. Political participation is active engagement, not passive withdrawal from the political process.

questions.text: A major reason for the adoption of a federal system in Nigeria was the
options: Existence of a homogeneous population with a single culture
Need to manage the country's diverse ethnic and linguistic groups
Desire to create a powerful central government that controls everything
Influence of the British colonial government which preferred a unitary system
questions.explanation: Nigeria's ethnic, linguistic, and religious diversity was the primary reason for adopting federalism, as it allows for the sharing of power between central and regional governments to accommodate diverse interests and prevent domination by any single group. The population is heterogeneous, and the British initially favoured a unitary system but conceded to federalism due to diversity.

questions.text: The principle of 'collective security' in international relations implies that
options: An attack on one state is considered an attack on all states that have agreed to the principle
Only the United States can guarantee global security
States must form regional alliances for self-defence
questions.explanation: Collective security is a system in which states agree to take collective action against any state that threatens or breaches international peace. The key idea is that aggression against one is aggression against all, and the international community will respond jointly. It does not require complete disarmament, is not limited to the US, and is broader than regional alliances.

questions.text: The head of the executive branch in a presidential system of government is the
questions.explanation: In a presidential system, the President is the head of the executive branch and is elected separately from the legislature. The Prime Minister is head of government in a parliamentary system, the Speaker is the presiding officer of the legislature, and the Chief Justice is head of the judiciary.

questions.text: A major factor that led to the formation of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) was the
options: Desire to create a single political federation for West Africa
Need to promote economic cooperation and integration among West African countries
Pressure from the United Nations to form a regional bloc
Requirement to establish a common military force to fight colonialism
questions.explanation: ECOWAS was established primarily to foster economic cooperation and integration among West African states through the removal of trade barriers, free movement of persons, and harmonisation of policies. While political federation and a military component (ECOMOG) are part of its evolution, the primary driver was economic cooperation.

questions.text: The concept of 'rule of law' was popularised by the British legal scholar
questions.explanation: A.V. Dicey is credited with popularising the concept of the rule of law in his classic work 'An Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution' (1885). He articulated its three main principles: supremacy of law, equality before the law, and the predominance of legal spirit. Locke and Hobbes are social contract theorists, and Bentham is associated with utilitarianism.

questions.text: A key feature of the Nigerian 1979 Constitution was the
options: Adoption of a parliamentary system of government
Introduction of the presidential system with a separation of powers
Establishment of a military council as the supreme governing body
Creation of a unicameral legislature at the federal level
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution was a landmark that adopted the US-style presidential system, featuring a directly elected president, a clear separation of powers, and a bicameral legislature. It replaced the parliamentary system of the First Republic. It did not establish military rule or a unicameral legislature.

questions.text: The term 'foreign policy' refers to the
options: Internal policies of a state towards its citizens
Strategies and actions a state employs in its relations with other states
Economic policies aimed at controlling inflation
Legal framework for the operation of local governments
questions.explanation: Foreign policy is the set of strategies, principles, and actions that a state adopts to achieve its objectives in its interactions with other international actors. It is distinct from domestic policies, economic policies (which may have internal dimensions), and local government frameworks.

questions.text: A major challenge to the effectiveness of the United Nations is the
options: Unanimity of the Security Council on all issues
Veto power of the five permanent members of the Security Council
Excessive power of the General Assembly
Lack of any judicial body to resolve international disputes
questions.explanation: The veto power held by the P5 (US, UK, France, Russia, China) is a significant challenge to UN effectiveness because it can paralyse the Security Council, preventing action even when there is broad international consensus. The General Assembly's powers are limited, and the International Court of Justice exists as a judicial body.

questions.text: The concept of 'political socialisation' is the process by which
options: Political parties select their candidates for elections
Citizens acquire their political values, beliefs, and attitudes
questions.explanation: Political socialisation is the lifelong process through which individuals internalise political knowledge, values, and orientations, shaping their political identity. This occurs through agents like family, schools, media, and peer groups. It is distinct from candidate selection, policy implementation, and judicial interpretation.

questions.text: The principle of 'separation of powers' is designed to
options: Concentrate all governmental power in the executive
Prevent the abuse of power by distributing it among different branches
Eliminate the need for a judiciary
Give unlimited authority to the legislature
questions.explanation: The separation of powers is a doctrine that divides governmental authority among the legislative, executive, and judicial branches to prevent any one branch from becoming too powerful and to provide checks and balances. It distributes power rather than concentrating it, and it reinforces the need for an independent judiciary.

questions.text: The African Union's Peace and Security Council is responsible for
options: Preventing and managing conflicts on the African continent
questions.explanation: The Peace and Security Council (PSC) is the standing decision-making organ of the AU for the prevention, management, and resolution of conflicts. It is the African equivalent of the UN Security Council. Trade promotion, currency unification, and election conduct are handled by other AU organs or member states.

questions.text: A major reason for the creation of local governments in Nigeria is to
options: Provide a platform for the central government to control all local affairs
Bring government closer to the people and facilitate grassroots development
Eliminate the authority of traditional rulers
Create a parallel administrative system to the state governments
questions.explanation: Local governments are established to bring administration and services closer to the people at the grassroots level, allowing for community participation in governance and local development. They are not designed to concentrate power at the centre, eliminate traditional rulers, or create a parallel state system.

questions.text: The term 'political ideology' refers to a
options: Set of beliefs and values that justify the exercise of power and guide political action
Legal document that outlines the structure of government
List of candidates for an election
questions.explanation: A political ideology is a coherent set of ideas, values, and beliefs that provides a framework for understanding how society should be organised and governed. It guides political action and justifies the exercise of power. It is distinct from constitutions, economic plans, or candidate lists.

questions.text: The main function of the National Assembly in Nigeria is to
options: Make laws and provide oversight over the executive
questions.explanation: The National Assembly's primary functions are law-making (legislation) and providing oversight of the executive to ensure accountability and proper implementation of policies. Implementation is the executive's role, adjudication is the judiciary's, and foreign policy is primarily an executive function.

questions.text: The concept of 'good governance' is characterised by
options: Absence of any form of public accountability
High levels of corruption and impunity
Transparency, accountability, and the rule of law
Concentration of power in a single ruler
questions.explanation: Good governance is defined by principles such as transparency, accountability, rule of law, participation, and responsiveness. It is the opposite of corruption, impunity, and the concentration of power without checks. These principles ensure that government actions are open, responsible, and just.

questions.text: A major feature of the Westminster model of government is the
options: Strict separation of powers between the executive and the legislature
Fusion of powers between the executive and the legislative branches
Direct election of the head of government by the people
Ceremonial role of the prime minister
questions.explanation: The Westminster model, or parliamentary system, is characterised by a fusion of powers, where the executive (Prime Minister and Cabinet) is drawn from and accountable to the legislature. This is in contrast to the separation of powers in the presidential system. The head of government is not directly elected by the people, and the Prime Minister is not ceremonial.

questions.text: The principle of 'diplomatic immunity' is based on the idea that
options: Diplomats are above the law of the host country
Diplomats must be allowed to carry out their functions without interference
Diplomats can vote in the host country's elections
Diplomats are exempt from all taxes in their own country
questions.explanation: Diplomatic immunity is a principle of international law that protects diplomats from legal action in the host country to ensure they can perform their duties freely and without fear of harassment or coercion. It is not about being above the law in a moral sense, but about functional necessity. It does not grant voting rights or full tax exemption.

questions.text: The primary purpose of the Nigerian Civil Service is to
options: Implement government policies and provide continuity in administration
questions.explanation: The civil service is the permanent bureaucracy responsible for implementing government decisions and policies, advising ministers, and ensuring continuity of administration regardless of changes in government. It is non-partisan and does not formulate partisan policy, adjudicate disputes, or make laws.

questions.text: The concept of 'political culture' is important because it
options: Determines the economic performance of a state
Shapes the attitudes of citizens towards their political system and influences political behaviour
Replaces the need for a written constitution
Is synonymous with the legal system
questions.explanation: Political culture comprises the shared beliefs, values, and attitudes of a society towards politics. It is important because it shapes how citizens perceive their political system, their level of participation, and their expectations of government. It does not determine economic performance directly, replace constitutions, or equate to the legal system.

questions.text: A major challenge to the implementation of federalism in Nigeria is the
options: Existence of a strong and impartial judiciary
Agitation for resource control and revenue allocation
Absence of ethnic and religious diversity
questions.explanation: A persistent challenge in Nigeria's federalism is the intense competition among states over the control and sharing of revenue from natural resources, particularly oil. This has led to political tensions, conflicts, and demands for greater autonomy. Nigeria is not homogeneous; its diversity is the source of many federal challenges.

questions.text: The head of government in the United Kingdom's parliamentary system is the
options: Speaker of the House of Commons
questions.explanation: In the UK, the Prime Minister is the head of government, leading the executive and holding the most political power. The Monarch is the ceremonial head of state, the Speaker presides over the House of Commons, and the Lord Chancellor has a judicial and ceremonial role.

questions.text: The concept of 'popular sovereignty' means that
options: The government is the ultimate source of all power
The people are the ultimate source of political authority
The judiciary has supreme power over the state
The military controls the political system
questions.explanation: Popular sovereignty is the principle that the authority of a state and its government is created and sustained by the consent of its people, through their elected representatives. It means the people are the ultimate source of political power. It is not about government self-authority, judicial supremacy, or military control.

questions.text: A major reason for the establishment of the United Nations was to
options: Promote the interests of the victorious powers after World War II
Prevent future wars and promote international cooperation
Establish a global government with binding authority
Create a military alliance against the Soviet Union
questions.explanation: The UN was founded in 1945 primarily to prevent the recurrence of devastating world wars and to foster international cooperation on issues like peace, security, human rights, and development. While it was influenced by the victorious powers, its stated purpose was broader and idealistic, not a global government or a specific anti-Soviet alliance.

questions.text: The term 'political obligation' refers to the
options: Right of the state to suspend all civil liberties
Duty of citizens to obey the laws of the state
Obligation of the government to provide free healthcare
Responsibility of the judiciary to interpret laws
questions.explanation: Political obligation is the moral or legal duty of citizens to obey the laws and support the institutions of the state. It is a cornerstone of political order and citizenship. It is not about state powers of suspension, government service provision (though related to rights), or judicial responsibility.

questions.text: The first military coup in Nigeria took place in
questions.explanation: The first military coup in Nigeria occurred on January 15, 1966, when a group of young army officers overthrew the civilian government of the First Republic. 1960 was the year of independence, 1975 was the coup that overthrew Gowon, and 1983 was the coup that overthrew Shagari.

questions.text: The concept of 'checks and balances' allows the legislature to
questions.explanation: Checks and balances give each branch of government some measure of control over the others. The legislature's power to approve (confirm) presidential appointments is a classic check on the executive. Implementation, interpretation, and foreign affairs are not primary legislative checks.

questions.text: A major feature of the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria is the
options: Provision for a parliamentary system of government
Establishment of a federal system with a bicameral legislature
Creation of a unitary state with a single legislature
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution establishes a federal system with a bicameral legislature (National Assembly) at the centre. It explicitly rejects a parliamentary system and a unitary state, and it maintains an independent judiciary.

questions.text: The term 'civil society' refers to
options: The government and its administrative agencies
Voluntary organisations and associations that operate outside the state
questions.explanation: Civil society is the sphere of voluntary collective action, including non-governmental organisations (NGOs), community groups, trade unions, and other associations that act independently of the state. It is distinct from the government, the military, and formal political parties, though they may interact.

questions.text: A major objective of the Nigerian foreign policy is to
options: Promote African unity and protect Nigeria's national interests
Align exclusively with the Western powers
Establish Nigeria as a global military superpower
questions.explanation: Nigeria's foreign policy is guided by a commitment to African unity, cooperation, and the protection of its national interests. This is reflected in the 'Concentric Circles' policy, which prioritises Africa. Isolation, exclusive alignment with any bloc, or military superpower status are not stated objectives.

questions.text: The concept of 'judicial independence' is essential because it ensures that
options: Judges are accountable to the executive
The judiciary can be influenced by political parties
Courts can adjudicate disputes fairly and impartially without external interference
Judges are appointed based on their political loyalty
questions.explanation: Judicial independence means that courts and judges operate free from influence from the executive, legislature, or other external pressures. This is essential for ensuring fair trials, upholding the rule of law, and protecting citizens' rights. Accountability to the executive or political influence would undermine this independence.

questions.text: The African Union was established in
questions.explanation: The African Union was established in 2002 as the successor to the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), which was founded in 1963. The OAU was transformed into the AU in 2002 to give it a more robust mandate for integration and development. 1980 and 1994 are not the founding years.

questions.text: The principle of 'non-interference' in international law means that
options: States can intervene in the internal affairs of other states for any reason
States should not interfere in the internal affairs of other sovereign states
The United Nations can intervene in any state without consent
States must intervene to protect human rights in other countries
questions.explanation: The principle of non-interference is a cornerstone of international law and state sovereignty, meaning that states should refrain from intervening in the internal matters of other states. While there are exceptions (e.g., humanitarian intervention or UN action), the general rule is non-interference. The other options contradict this fundamental principle.

questions.text: A major function of the legislature is the
options: Power of the purse (control over public finances)
questions.explanation: The power of the purse, or the legislature's authority to approve government expenditures and taxation, is a key function of the legislature, serving as a check on the executive. Execution is executive, interpretation is judicial, and foreign policy is primarily executive.

questions.text: The concept of 'political party system' refers to the
options: Internal structure of a single political party
Number of political parties in a country and their relationship
Electoral laws governing the conduct of elections
Ideological orientation of the ruling party
questions.explanation: A party system describes the configuration of parties in a country, including the number of parties (e.g., one-party, two-party, multi-party) and the nature of their interaction (e.g., competitive, dominant, or fragmented). It is not about a single party's structure, electoral laws, or ideology, though these influence the system.

questions.text: The primary reason for the creation of the Nigerian Petroleum Resources Development Company (NPDC) was to
options: Privatise all oil assets in Nigeria
Develop and manage the country's oil and gas resources effectively
Eliminate all foreign oil companies from Nigeria
Create a monopoly for the distribution of petroleum products
questions.explanation: The NPDC is a subsidiary of the NNPC established to pursue aggressive exploration and development of oil and gas resources to increase the country's reserves and production. It is not for privatisation, eliminating foreign companies, or creating a monopoly for distribution, though it plays a role in the upstream sector.

questions.text: The concept of 'political stability' is achieved when
options: There is a frequent change of government
The government is able to maintain order and continuity despite challenges
The military is in complete control of the state
questions.explanation: Political stability refers to a state of order, continuity, and predictability in governance, where the government can effectively manage conflicts, maintain law and order, and ensure smooth transitions of power. Frequent changes, military control, or the absence of opposition are not indicators of stability in a democratic sense.

questions.text: A major feature of the traditional Yoruba political system was the
options: Highly centralised authority of the Alaafin of Oyo with a council of chiefs
Decentralised system based on village assemblies
Absence of any formal political institutions
Theocratic rule by the Ooni of Ife over all Yoruba land
questions.explanation: The Yoruba political system, particularly the Oyo Empire, was highly centralised under the Alaafin (king), who was assisted by a council of chiefs, the Oyo Mesi, and the Ogboni society. The Alaafin's authority was significant but checked by the council. It was not decentralised like the Igbo system, nor was it theocratic in the sense of a priestly rule, though the Ooni held spiritual authority.

questions.text: The United Nations Security Council has how many non-permanent members
questions.explanation: The UN Security Council has 15 members in total: 5 permanent members (P5) with veto power and 10 non-permanent members elected for two-year terms. The non-permanent members are elected by the General Assembly. The total is 15, so the number of non-permanent members is 10.

questions.text: The concept of 'public opinion' is most effectively expressed through
options: Free and fair elections, opinion polls, and a vibrant media
questions.explanation: Public opinion is the collective views of the people on political and social issues. It is best expressed and measured through mechanisms like free elections (where citizens vote), opinion polls, and a free media that allows for debate and expression. Government decrees, judicial decisions, and traditional rulers' pronouncements do not necessarily reflect public opinion.

questions.text: The main purpose of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) in Nigeria is to
options: Provide military training for all graduates
Foster national unity and integration by posting graduates to different states
Employ all university graduates after their studies
Promote vocational skills for unskilled youths
questions.explanation: The NYSC was established in 1973 to develop a sense of national unity and integration by deploying young graduates to serve in states other than their own, thereby encouraging cross-cultural interaction and understanding. It is not primarily for military training, employment (though it involves service), or vocational skills for unskilled youth.

questions.text: A fundamental feature of a state that distinguishes it from other forms of political association is the possession of
options: A monopoly over the legitimate use of physical force within a defined territory
A written constitution that guarantees fundamental human rights
A democratically elected legislature that makes all laws
A ceremonial head of state who serves as a symbol of national unity
questions.explanation: The state is uniquely defined by its sovereign authority and the monopoly on the legitimate use of coercion, as articulated by Max Weber. While many states have constitutions, legislatures, or heads of state, these are not universal or defining features. The monopoly on force is what gives the state its ultimate authority over all other associations within its borders.

questions.text: The doctrine of separation of powers is primarily designed to prevent
options: The excessive concentration of governmental authority in one body
The overlap of functions between the executive and the judiciary
The influence of political parties on the legislative process
The delegation of legislative powers to administrative agencies
questions.explanation: The separation of powers, as articulated by Montesquieu, aims to divide government into distinct branches (legislative, executive, judicial) to avoid tyranny from concentrated power. Overlap is not the primary concern, nor is the influence of parties or delegation of powers, which can occur even within separate branches. The core goal is to create checks and balances by distributing power.

questions.text: A major weakness of the Unitary system of government is that it
options: Tends to be slow in responding to local emergencies
Encourages the proliferation of political parties
Makes the central government too distant and unresponsive to local needs
questions.explanation: In a unitary system, all major powers are concentrated in the central government, which can lead to insensitivity to local peculiarities and a slow response to local issues. It does not promote regional autonomy; that is a feature of federalism. It does not inherently encourage party proliferation and can be swift in decision-making, though not necessarily responsive.

questions.text: The concept of political sovereignty refers to the
options: Legal authority to make and enforce final decisions within a state
Moral right of citizens to rebel against an oppressive government
Economic power held by multinational corporations within a country
Social influence of religious institutions over state policies
questions.explanation: Political sovereignty is the ultimate, absolute, and indivisible source of power in a state, residing in the state itself. This authority is legally recognised and entails the power to make binding decisions. Moral rights, economic power, and social influence are separate concepts, not the definition of political sovereignty, which is legal and final.

questions.text: A constitution is considered rigid if its amendment process
options: Requires a simple majority vote in the legislature
Is more complex and difficult than the ordinary legislative process
Is left entirely to the discretion of the executive branch
Can be initiated only by the judiciary
questions.explanation: A rigid constitution has a special, more cumbersome amendment procedure than ordinary laws, requiring, for example, supermajorities or referendums. A simple majority denotes a flexible constitution. Amendment is typically a legislative or popular act, not executive or judicial, so options C and D are incorrect.

questions.text: The primary function of the legislature in a democratic system is to
options: Implement and enforce the laws of the land
Interpret the constitution and adjudicate disputes
Make laws and represent the interests of the people
Appoint the head of government and the cabinet
questions.explanation: The core function of the legislature is law-making and representation of citizens. Implementation is the function of the executive, interpretation is the judiciary's role, and appointment of the head of government is typically an executive or ceremonial function, not the primary purpose of the legislature.

questions.text: A system of government where the executive branch is fused with the legislative branch is known as
questions.explanation: In a parliamentary system, the executive (Prime Minister and Cabinet) are drawn from and accountable to the legislature, indicating a fusion of powers. In contrast, a presidential system has a strict separation of powers. Federal and confederal systems describe territorial distribution of power, not the executive-legislative relationship.

questions.text: The principle of collective responsibility in a cabinet system implies that
options: Ministers must publicly support government decisions or resign
Each minister is solely responsible for his or her own ministry
The cabinet is responsible to the judiciary for its actions
Decisions are made by majority vote in the cabinet
questions.explanation: Collective responsibility means that all cabinet members are bound by and must publicly defend all government decisions, even if they personally disagree, or they must resign. It does not imply individual ministerial responsibility, nor accountability to the judiciary, and while decisions may be by majority, the core principle is the public solidarity of the cabinet.

questions.text: A vital characteristic of a federal constitution is the
options: Supremacy of the central government over all other levels
Existence of a single, unified legal system for the entire country
Division of powers between the central and regional governments
Unicameral legislature at the national level
questions.explanation: A federal constitution is defined by the constitutional division of powers between a national (central) government and regional (state/provincial) governments, each being autonomous in their own spheres. Supremacy of the centre is a feature of a unitary state, not federalism. Federal systems often have bicameral legislatures and multiple legal systems.

questions.text: A major factor that necessitated the creation of local government in Nigeria is the
options: Desire to weaken the power of the central government
Need to bring governance closer to the people at the grassroots
Requirement to implement the policies of international organisations
Directive from the traditional rulers to create more chieftaincies
questions.explanation: The primary rationale for local government is to ensure grassroots participation and bring government services and administration closer to the people. Its creation is not to weaken the centre, but to complement it, and it is not driven by international dictates or traditional rulers, though they may be involved.

questions.text: During the colonial era in Nigeria, the system of indirect rule was most effectively implemented in the
options: Eastern region with its centralised Igbo political system
Northern region with its established Emirate system
Western region with its complex Oyo Empire structure
Lagos Colony due to its high concentration of European settlers
questions.explanation: Indirect rule, as pioneered by Lord Lugard, was most successful in Northern Nigeria because it utilised the existing, centralised, and hierarchical Emirate system for administration. The Igbo political system was decentralised and stateless, making it difficult to apply. The Western region had some success but was more complex, and Lagos was under direct rule.

questions.text: A key demand of the Nigerian nationalist movement was the
options: Immediate abolition of all traditional institutions
Establishment of a military government to oversee independence
Replacement of the colonial administration with an elected African majority government
Creation of a federation based solely on ethnic lines
questions.explanation: The core goal of Nigerian nationalism was political independence, which meant the transfer of power from the colonial administration to an elected government controlled by the African majority. Nationalists did not seek to abolish traditional institutions entirely nor impose military rule, and while federalism was considered, it was not based solely on ethnicity.

questions.text: The 1979 Constitution of Nigeria introduced the presidential system of government primarily to
options: Emulate the British Westminster model of governance
Ensure a fusion of powers between the executive and the legislature
Prevent the concentration of power and provide for a separation of powers
Strengthen the role of traditional rulers in national politics
questions.explanation: The 1979 Constitution was designed to replace the British parliamentary system with a US-style presidential system to diffuse power and prevent the instability and abuse seen in previous republics. The system was created to ensure a clear separation of powers. It did not aim for fusion, nor was its primary purpose to strengthen traditional rulers.

questions.text: The concept of judicial independence is crucial in a democracy because it ensures that
options: Judges are appointed based on their political party affiliation
The judiciary acts as an impartial arbiter in disputes, free from executive or legislative pressure
The court system operates under the direct supervision of the Ministry of Justice
Judges are accountable to the electorate through periodic elections
questions.explanation: Judicial independence means courts can adjudicate matters without interference from the other branches of government. This is vital for upholding the rule of law and protecting citizens' rights. Independence is violated if judges are chosen by party affiliation or are under the thumb of the executive. Accountability through elections can undermine independence.

questions.text: A by-election is held to fill a vacant seat in the legislature that arises due to
options: The end of the normal term of the legislative house
A general election called by the president
The death or resignation of an incumbent member
A successful vote of no confidence in the government
questions.explanation: A by-election is a special election held between general elections to fill a specific vacancy caused by the death, resignation, or disqualification of a sitting legislator. The end of a term is not a by-election but a general election. A vote of no confidence would typically lead to a change in government, not a by-election for an individual seat.

questions.text: Pressure groups differ from political parties in that pressure groups
options: Seek to capture political power by contesting elections
Are primarily concerned with influencing government policy without directly seeking to form a government
Are always ideologically driven and have a broad manifesto
Have a more extensive organisational structure than political parties
questions.explanation: Pressure groups are distinct from political parties in that they do not aim to form a government. Their objective is to exert influence on those in power to adopt specific policies. Parties contest elections and seek office. Pressure groups can be ideological but are often single-issue focused, and they typically have a narrower, more fluid structure.

questions.text: The main reason for the creation of the Federation of Nigeria in 1914 was to
options: Promote the cultural integration of the various ethnic groups
Establish a single administrative unit for economic convenience and security
Prepare the territory for immediate self-governance
Divide the territory into equal administrative regions
questions.explanation: The amalgamation of the Northern and Southern Protectorates in 1914 was driven primarily by British administrative and economic interests. It was cheaper to administer one entity and facilitated the control of trade routes, notably the Niger River. It was not for cultural integration nor self-governance, which came later, nor for equal division.

questions.text: A key feature of the 1963 Republican Constitution of Nigeria was the
options: Establishment of Nigeria as a republic within the British Commonwealth
Abolition of all regional governments in favour of a unitary state
Creation of a directly elected executive president with vast powers
Introduction of a parliamentary system of government
questions.explanation: The 1963 Constitution declared Nigeria a republic, replacing the British monarch with a Nigerian President as ceremonial head of state, while remaining in the Commonwealth. It did not abolish regional governments; they were strengthened. It did not create a directly elected executive president; that came later. The parliamentary system was already in place.

questions.text: The concept of the 'rule of law' implies that
options: All citizens, including government officials, are subject to the law
The laws made by the legislature are always just and equitable
The executive branch can suspend the law in times of emergency
Only the judiciary has the authority to interpret the law
questions.explanation: The rule of law, as defined by A.V. Dicey, means the absolute supremacy of regular law as opposed to arbitrary power, and equality before the law for all, including officials. Laws are not automatically just, emergencies have legal procedures, and while judicial interpretation is a part, the core is universal subjection to law.

questions.text: A public corporation is typically established by an act of parliament to
options: Provide essential services to the public at subsidised rates
Engage in commercial activities in direct competition with private firms
Advise the government on economic policy
questions.explanation: Public corporations are statutory bodies created to provide essential public services (like water, electricity) that may not be profitable but are socially necessary. They are not profit-driven for shareholders; they are state-owned. They are not primarily for policy advice, that is the role of commissions or advisory bodies.

questions.text: The main function of the Civil Service in a modern state is to
options: Advise the executive and implement its decisions
Represent the people in the legislature
questions.explanation: The civil service is the permanent bureaucracy that implements the policies and decisions of the elected government and provides expert advice to ministers. Formulating policy is primarily the role of the political executive, representation is for legislators, and adjudication is for the judiciary.

questions.text: A major problem facing federal systems of government, including Nigeria, is the
options: Difficulty in achieving a balanced and equitable distribution of resources among the federating units
Dominance of the judicial branch over the other two branches
Excessive power of local governments over the central government
questions.explanation: A persistent challenge in federalism is the distribution of financial resources and developmental projects among states, often leading to contention and perceptions of marginalization. Federal systems generally have written constitutions, and the judiciary is not dominant; power is meant to be shared. Local governments are subordinate to the state and federal levels.

questions.text: The electoral system in which the candidate with the highest number of votes, even if not a majority, is declared the winner is known as
questions.explanation: The First-Past-The-Post (FPTP) system, also known as a plurality system, awards victory to the candidate with the most votes, regardless of whether they exceed 50%. The Second Ballot involves a run-off if no majority is achieved. The List System is a form of proportional representation. Alternative Vote uses preferential ranking.

questions.text: The concept of a 'lame duck' session in a presidential system refers to a period when
options: The legislature is prorogued by the president
An outgoing president has reduced political influence after an election defeat
A new president has not yet been inaugurated
The judiciary has declared a law unconstitutional
questions.explanation: The term 'lame duck' describes an elected official, especially a president, who is in the final period of office after a successor has been elected but before the successor takes office. Their political power is diminished because they are not seeking reelection. It is not related to prorogation, the interregnum, or judicial review.

questions.text: The African Union (AU) was founded primarily to
options: Create a single African state under a central government
Promote economic integration and political cooperation among African states
Replace the United Nations in all African affairs
Establish a common African military command to defend against external aggression
questions.explanation: The African Union was established as the successor to the OAU with a focus on greater economic integration, political cooperation, peace, and security, and to accelerate the political and socio-economic integration of the continent. It does not aim to create a single state, nor does it replace the UN.

questions.text: The resolution of inter-state conflicts through dialogue and peaceful negotiation is a fundamental principle of
questions.explanation: The United Nations Charter, in Chapter I, Article 1, states its purpose is to maintain international peace and security and to take effective measures for the prevention and removal of threats to the peace through peaceful means. NATO is a military alliance, WTO deals with trade, and IMF with financial stability.

questions.text: A major difference between a state and a nation is that a state
options: Is a political unit with defined boundaries and a government, whereas a nation is a group of people with a common identity
Is always sovereign, whereas a nation never has sovereignty
Is based on ethnic ties, whereas a nation is based on a shared territory
Is a cultural entity, whereas a nation is a legal entity
questions.explanation: The key distinction is that the state is a legal-political entity with defined borders and a system of government, while a nation is a group of people bound by shared history, culture, language, or ethnicity. A nation is not always sovereign (e.g., the Kurdish nation), and a state is not necessarily a nation-state.

questions.text: The principle of checks and balances is often operationalised in a presidential system by
options: The legislature having the power to impeach the president
The executive appointing judges without legislative confirmation
The judiciary having the power to dissolve the legislature
The president having the authority to override judicial rulings
questions.explanation: Checks and balances allow each branch to exercise oversight and limit the power of others. The legislature's power to impeach the president is a primary check on the executive. Executive appointment of judges often requires confirmation (a check). The judiciary cannot dissolve the legislature, and the president cannot override judicial rulings.

questions.text: The action of a sovereign state that infringes on the territorial integrity of another state is a violation of the
options: Principle of non-intervention in domestic affairs
questions.explanation: The principle of non-intervention is a cornerstone of international law, prohibiting states from interfering in the internal or external affairs of other states, especially the use of force or territorial violation. State succession deals with replacement of states, self-determination is about peoples' rights, and diplomatic immunity is about protecting diplomats.

questions.text: A key feature of the traditional Hausa-Fulani political system was the
options: Strongly centralised authority of the Emir with a hierarchy of officials
Decentralised system based on village councils and age grades
Complex system of checks and balances similar to a presidential system
Absence of any formal political institutions
questions.explanation: The Hausa-Fulani political system was highly centralised, with the Emir as the supreme political, religious, and judicial authority, assisted by a series of officials (e.g., Waziri, Galadima). This is in stark contrast to the more decentralised Igbo system. It was a pre-colonial monarchy, not a modern presidential one.

questions.text: The right to vote and be voted for is a fundamental feature of
questions.explanation: Political participation involves all activities by which citizens attempt to influence the selection of political leaders and the policies they pursue. Voting is the most basic and widespread form of this participation. Apathy is the opposite, socialisation is the learning process, and obligation is the duty to obey the state.

questions.text: A government's policy of protecting domestic industries from foreign competition through tariffs and quotas is known as
questions.explanation: Protectionism is the economic policy of restraining trade between states through methods like tariffs, quotas, and subsidies to protect local businesses. Free trade is the opposite, deregulation is removing government controls, and privatisation is transferring ownership from state to private sector.

questions.text: The immediate cause of the Nigerian Civil War (1967-1970) was the
options: Massacre of Easterners in the North in 1966 and the subsequent declaration of Biafra
questions.explanation: While the 1966 coups set the stage, the immediate trigger was the pogrom against Easterners in the North, which led to the return of Easterners to their home region and the subsequent declaration of the Republic of Biafra by Lt. Col. Ojukwu on May 30, 1967. The Western crisis and election annulments were earlier preludes, not the direct cause.

questions.text: The primary role of the military in a democratic society, according to the principle of civil-military relations, is to
options: Protect the state from external and internal threats, and remain subordinate to civilian authority
Act as a check on the power of the executive branch
Participate in partisan politics and contest elections
questions.explanation: The core tenet of civil-military relations is that the military is the ultimate guarantor of state security but must be firmly under the control of democratically elected civilian leadership. It does not make policy (the government does), nor does it act as a political check or participate in partisan elections.

questions.text: The political party system in Nigeria between 1999 and 2023 is best described as
questions.explanation: Since the return to democracy in 1999, Nigeria has operated a multi-party system, with numerous political parties competing for electoral office. While the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and All Progressives Congress (APC) have been dominant, other parties like the SDP, AD, APGA, and NNPP have existed, making it a multi-party system, not a strict two-party one.

questions.text: A significant challenge facing the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) is the
options: Existence of a single currency for all member states
Lack of a common language for communication
Issue of implementing protocols and ensuring compliance by member states
Absence of a conflict resolution mechanism
questions.explanation: ECOWAS faces the chronic problem of implementation and compliance. Member states often sign protocols (e.g., on free movement or trade) but struggle to enforce or incorporate them into national law. While a single currency (the Eco) is a goal, its absence is not the core challenge. ECOWAS has conflict resolution mechanisms like ECOMOG.

questions.text: The concept of 'majority rule' in a democracy is most effectively protected by
options: The unrestricted power of the majority party in parliament
A constitutional framework that also protects minority rights
The abolition of all non-governmental organisations
questions.explanation: A healthy democracy balances majority rule with the protection of minority rights, as enshrined in a constitution that provides fundamental freedoms and judicial review. This prevents the 'tyranny of the majority'. Unrestricted majority power can lead to oppression, while direct democracy has its own pitfalls.

questions.text: A key feature of the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria is the
options: Establishment of a parliamentary system of government
Creation of six geo-political zones as distinct administrative units
Provision for a bicameral legislature at the federal level
Abolition of state governments in favour of a unitary state
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution established the National Assembly, which is bicameral, consisting of the Senate and the House of Representatives. It established a presidential system (not parliamentary), and while it recognises six geo-political zones, they are not constitutional administrative units, and the state governments are constitutionally established.

questions.text: The act of deliberately distorting electoral results to favour a particular candidate or party is known as
questions.explanation: Electoral fraud is the specific and intentional act of illegally interfering with the process of an election, which includes ballot-stuffing, vote-buying, and manipulating the count. Maladministration is more about poor management, violence is intimidation, and apathy is voter disinterest.

questions.text: An important feature of the pre-colonial Igbo political system was its
options: Highly centralised monarchy with a powerful king
Republican and decentralised nature based on the village assembly
Feudal system based on land ownership by a few nobles
Theocratic system ruled by a powerful priestly class
questions.explanation: The Igbo political system is famously described as a segmentary, acephalous (headless) society. It was decentralised, with the village or town assembly (Oha) serving as the primary decision-making body, and authority was dispersed among various lineage and title-holding groups. It lacked a centralised monarchy.

questions.text: The term 'sovereignty' in international law is often limited in practice by the
options: Ability of a state to enforce its laws without exception
Growing influence of international organisations and treaties that bind state behaviour
Absolute power of a state over its domestic affairs
Right of a state to wage war against another state
questions.explanation: While sovereignty implies supreme authority, in practice it is constrained by international law, treaties, and membership in international organisations like the UN and AU, which impose obligations. A state's power is not absolute if it has agreed to be bound by international norms. The other options are traditional, unqualified aspects of sovereignty.

questions.text: The system of government in which the executive and the legislature are both directly elected by the people and are constitutionally independent of each other is the
questions.explanation: In a presidential system, the president is elected separately from the legislature (often directly by the people) and serves a fixed term, making the executive independent. The parliamentary system (or Cabinet/Westminster) has the executive drawn from and dependent on the legislature.

questions.text: A major objective of the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons (NCNC) was the
options: Establishment of a unitary state for Nigeria
Protection of the rights and interests of the Igbo ethnic group and the struggle for independence
Creation of an Islamic caliphate in Northern Nigeria
Promotion of British colonial rule as a permanent institution
questions.explanation: The NCNC, led by figures like Nnamdi Azikiwe, was a nationalist party that sought to unify the various groups, particularly in the East, to fight for self-government and protect the rights of Igbos. It did not advocate for a unitary state or an Islamic caliphate, and it opposed colonial rule.

questions.text: The principle that all citizens, irrespective of their status, are subject to the same laws and courts is a key component of the
questions.explanation: This is the principle of equality before the law, which is a core pillar of the rule of law. It means no one is above the law, and all are subject to the ordinary law courts. Separation of powers is about branch relationships, justice is a broader concept, and federalism is about power distribution.

questions.text: The process through which individuals acquire political attitudes, values, and beliefs is called
questions.explanation: Political socialisation is the lifelong process by which people form their ideas about politics and acquire political values. Mobilisation is getting people to act, recruitment is selecting candidates, and participation is the act of involvement itself.

questions.text: A major reason for the adoption of federalism in Nigeria was the
options: Homogeneous nature of the Nigerian population
Desire to create a powerful central government
Need to manage the country's vast ethnic and regional diversity
Influence of the British monarch who favoured a unitary system
questions.explanation: Nigeria adopted federalism primarily to accommodate its multi-ethnic, multi-lingual, and multi-religious diversity. A unitary system would have been difficult to govern effectively. The population is heterogeneous, the creation was to share power, not concentrate it, and the British initially governed under a unitary structure.

questions.text: The judicial review power of the Supreme Court allows it to
options: Review the performance of the executive branch
Determine the constitutionality of laws and executive actions
Amend the constitution without legislative approval
questions.explanation: Judicial review is the power of the Supreme Court to declare laws or actions of the executive unconstitutional if they violate the constitution. It does not review performance for efficiency, nor can it amend the constitution. That is a legislative function. Appointment of judges usually involves the executive and judicial councils.

questions.text: A 'whip' in a legislative assembly is a party official responsible for
options: Chairing the sessions of the house
Maintaining party discipline and ensuring members vote as directed
Representing the constituency in the cabinet
Leading the opposition in the parliament
questions.explanation: The whip is a party official whose role is to ensure party members attend debates and vote according to the party line. The speaker chairs sessions, the member represents the constituency, and the Leader of the Opposition leads the opposition. The whip's job is discipline and organisation.

questions.text: The main organ of the United Nations responsible for maintaining international peace and security is the
questions.explanation: The Security Council has primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security under the UN Charter. The General Assembly deliberates but its resolutions are recommendatory. ECOSOC handles social and economic issues, and the ICJ settles legal disputes between states.

questions.text: The concept of 'political culture' refers to the
options: Formal institutions of government within a state
Attitudes, beliefs, and values that underpin a political system
Economic policies adopted by a ruling party
Legal framework established by the constitution
questions.explanation: Political culture is the set of deeply held, widely shared beliefs, values, and attitudes that determine how a society's citizens relate to their political system. It is the subjective, psychological dimension of politics. Institutions, policies, and laws are the objective aspects, not the culture itself.

questions.text: The principle of 'federal character' in the Nigerian Constitution is designed to promote
options: The dominance of the largest ethnic group in all appointments
A uniform distribution of public offices among the various ethnic and geographical groups
The abolition of all state governments
The creation of a one-party state
questions.explanation: The federal character principle, enshrined in the 1999 Constitution, aims to ensure that appointments to public positions reflect the diverse ethnic, religious, and geographic composition of Nigeria. This prevents any group from monopolising power and promotes national unity. It does not promote ethnic dominance, abolish state governments, or create a one-party state.

questions.text: The theory of separation of powers was primarily developed to
options: Concentrate all authority in the executive for efficiency
Prevent tyranny by dividing governmental power among distinct branches
Eliminate the need for a judicial system
Grant unlimited authority to the legislature
questions.explanation: The separation of powers doctrine, articulated by Montesquieu, is designed to prevent the abuse of power and tyranny by ensuring that the legislative, executive, and judicial functions are distributed among separate and independent bodies. This creates a system of checks and balances. It is the opposite of concentrating power or eliminating branches.

questions.text: A major reason for the adoption of a unicameral legislature in some countries is the
options: Desire to create a more expensive and complex legislative process
Need for a faster and more efficient legislative decision-making process
Requirement to provide a check on the executive through a second chamber
Preference for a federal system of government
questions.explanation: Unicameral legislatures, consisting of a single chamber, are often adopted to simplify the legislative process, reduce costs, and speed up decision-making. They are common in smaller or more homogeneous states. A second chamber provides a check on the executive, which is the opposite rationale, and unicameralism is not inherently linked to federalism.

questions.text: The concept of 'political apathy' can be countered by
options: Increasing civic education and encouraging citizen participation
Restricting the freedom of the press
Concentrating power in a single ruler
questions.explanation: Political apathy, or indifference to politics, is often addressed through civic education that informs citizens about their rights and responsibilities, and through encouraging participation in elections and community activities. Restricting press freedom, eliminating parties, or concentrating power would likely increase apathy and alienation.

questions.text: A key feature of a federal system of government is the
options: Supremacy of regional governments over the central government
Constitutional division of powers between the central and regional governments
Complete absence of a central authority
Unitary control of all governmental functions
questions.explanation: The defining characteristic of federalism is the constitutional division of powers, where both the central (national) government and the regional (state) governments have their own areas of authority and autonomy. This is distinct from unitary systems (where power is centralised) and confederal systems (where regional governments are supreme).

questions.text: The Nigerian military's intervention in politics in 1966 was a departure from the
options: Parliamentary system that Nigeria had adopted at independence
Presidential system that was established in 1979
Confederal system that was proposed by the nationalist movements
Monarchical system that existed under colonial rule
questions.explanation: The 1966 military coup ended the parliamentary system (Westminster model) that Nigeria had operated since independence in 1960. The presidential system came later in 1979, and Nigeria never operated a confederal or monarchical system under colonial rule, as it was a colony directly administered by Britain.

questions.text: The Commonwealth of Nations is an association of
options: Countries that were all former colonies of France
Mostly former British colonies that have chosen to maintain ties
All countries that are members of the United Nations
questions.explanation: The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of 56 sovereign states, the vast majority of which are former territories of the British Empire. Membership is based on shared values and a common heritage. It is not limited to former French colonies, all UN members, or EU countries, though some members are also in these organisations.

questions.text: The concept of 'national interest' in foreign policy is often defined in terms of
options: The personal ambitions of the head of state
The security, economic prosperity, and territorial integrity of the state
The profit motives of multinational corporations
The cultural preferences of the ruling elite
questions.explanation: National interest encompasses the core goals a state seeks to achieve internationally, typically including security (protection from threats), economic well-being, and the preservation of territorial integrity and sovereignty. It is distinct from personal ambitions, corporate profits, or cultural preferences, though these may influence policy.

questions.text: A major challenge to the effective operation of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) is the
options: High level of economic integration achieved by member states
Lack of any protocol on free movement of persons
Failure of many member states to implement agreed protocols and decisions
Existence of a single currency for all member states
questions.explanation: A significant challenge to ECOWAS is the gap between signing protocols and actual implementation by member states. Many states fail to domesticate and enforce agreements on trade, free movement, and other areas, hindering integration. Free movement protocols do exist but are often poorly enforced, and a single currency is a long-term goal, not a current challenge.

questions.text: The primary function of the Civil Service in Nigeria is the
options: Implementation of government policies and provision of expert advice
Making of laws for the federation
questions.explanation: The Civil Service is the administrative machinery of the state, responsible for executing government policies, providing professional advice to ministers, and ensuring continuity in administration. It is non-partisan and does not formulate partisan policies, adjudicate disputes (judiciary), or make laws (legislature).

questions.text: The concept of 'political legitimacy' is closely related to the
options: Acceptance of the government's right to rule by the people
questions.explanation: Political legitimacy refers to the belief that the government has the right and moral authority to rule, based on the consent and acceptance of the governed. This can stem from legal processes, tradition, or charisma. It is distinct from military power, economic wealth, or international recognition, though these can support legitimacy.

questions.text: A major feature of the 1960 Independence Constitution of Nigeria was the
options: Establishment of a presidential system with a directly elected president
Retention of the British monarch as the ceremonial head of state
Creation of a unicameral legislature at the federal level
Abolition of the federal system of government
questions.explanation: The 1960 Constitution established Nigeria as an independent dominion within the Commonwealth, with the British Queen as the ceremonial head of state, represented by a Governor-General. It retained a parliamentary system and a federal structure with a bicameral legislature. The presidential system came later in 1979.

questions.text: The doctrine of 'ultra vires' in administrative law is used to
options: Approve actions taken by public bodies
Invalidate actions taken by public bodies that exceed their legal authority
Appoint judges to the Supreme Court
questions.explanation: Ultra vires (Latin for 'beyond the powers') is a legal principle used by courts to review and declare null and void any actions taken by public authorities that are not authorised by the statute that created them. This is a key check on administrative power, preventing abuse and ensuring that bodies act within their legal limits.

questions.text: A major objective of the Nigerian foreign policy of 'Concentric Circles' is to
options: Focus exclusively on relations with Western powers
Prioritise relations with Nigeria's immediate neighbours and the African continent
Establish Nigeria as the sole superpower in Africa
questions.explanation: The 'Concentric Circles' policy defines Nigeria's foreign policy priorities in layers: first its immediate neighbours and ECOWAS, then the wider African continent (AU), then the rest of the world. This reflects a commitment to African solidarity and regional integration. It does not prioritise the West, isolate Nigeria, or seek superpower status.

questions.text: The head of state in a parliamentary system is often
options: A ceremonial figure such as a monarch or a non-executive president
questions.explanation: In a parliamentary system, the head of state is usually a ceremonial figure (e.g., a constitutional monarch or a president with limited powers), while the head of government (the Prime Minister) exercises real political power. This is a key distinction from the presidential system, where the president is both head of state and head of government.

questions.text: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was established primarily to
options: Eradicate colonialism and promote unity among African states
Create a single African military command
questions.explanation: The OAU, founded in 1963, had as its primary objectives the eradication of colonialism and apartheid from the African continent and the promotion of unity and solidarity among African states. While economic development was a concern, it was not the exclusive focus. Military command and a common currency were not established at its founding.

questions.text: A major weakness of the presidential system of government is the
options: Fusion of powers between the executive and the legislature
Potential for a stalemate between the executive and the legislature
Absence of any checks and balances
Inability of the president to be removed from office
questions.explanation: A key weakness of the presidential system is the possibility of gridlock or stalemate when the executive and the legislature are controlled by different parties, making it difficult to pass legislation and leading to political conflict. It is not a fusion of powers (that is parliamentary), it has checks and balances, and the president can be removed through impeachment.

questions.text: The concept of 'civil society' is distinct from the state because it
options: Is an organ of the government
Operates independently of the state and is composed of voluntary associations
Is a branch of the judiciary
questions.explanation: Civil society refers to the sphere of voluntary organisations, NGOs, community groups, and other associations that exist independently of the state. It is a space for citizens to act collectively on issues of common concern, distinct from the formal institutions of government, the judiciary, or the military.

questions.text: The main purpose of the legislative oversight function is to
options: Reduce the budget of the executive
Ensure that the executive is implementing laws as intended
Appoint new members to the judiciary
Control the foreign policy of the state
questions.explanation: Oversight is the legislature's power to monitor and review the actions of the executive to ensure laws are being faithfully executed and public funds are used properly. It is not about reducing budgets (though it can), nor is it about judicial appointments or controlling foreign policy, though it may have influence.

questions.text: A major factor that necessitated the creation of the Mid-Western Region in Nigeria in 1963 was
options: The desire of the Igbo ethnic group to have a region of their own
The agitation of minority groups in the Western Region for their own state
The need to create a region for the Hausa-Fulani
The decision of the colonial administration to create more regions
questions.explanation: The Mid-Western Region was carved out of the Western Region in 1963 to address the political demands of minority groups (such as the Edo, Urhobo, and Itsekiri) who felt marginalised by the dominant Yoruba majority. It was not for the Igbo or Hausa-Fulani, and it was created after independence, not by the colonial administration.

questions.text: The principle of 'diplomatic immunity' in international relations is based on the
options: Need for diplomats to be exempt from all taxes in the host country
Functional necessity of ensuring diplomats can work without hindrance
Right of diplomats to vote in the host country's elections
Requirement that diplomats must be citizens of the host country
questions.explanation: Diplomatic immunity is grounded in the functional necessity theory, which holds that diplomats must be protected from legal action and harassment in the host country to perform their duties effectively. It is not about tax exemption (though it may be a part), voting rights, or citizenship requirements.

questions.text: The 1999 Constitution of Nigeria provides for a
options: Parliamentary system with a Prime Minister
Presidential system with a bicameral legislature
Unitary system with a single legislature
Confederal system with weak central government
questions.explanation: The 1999 Constitution establishes a presidential system of government at the federal level, with a directly elected president as head of state and government, and a bicameral National Assembly (Senate and House of Representatives). It does not provide for a parliamentary, unitary, or confederal system.

questions.text: A major challenge to the implementation of the rule of law in Nigeria is the
options: Widespread corruption and a weak legal infrastructure
Strong parliamentary oversight of the executive
Existence of a free and vigilant press
questions.explanation: Corruption and weak legal infrastructure are significant obstacles to the rule of law in Nigeria. They undermine the impartiality of the judiciary, encourage impunity, and erode public trust. Judicial independence, parliamentary oversight, and a free press would actually support, not challenge, the rule of law.

questions.text: The concept of 'political socialisation' is the process by which
options: Political parties select their candidates for elections
Citizens acquire their political values, beliefs, and attitudes
questions.explanation: Political socialisation is the lifelong process through which individuals internalise political knowledge, values, and orientations, shaping their political identity. This occurs through agents like family, schools, media, and peer groups. It is distinct from candidate selection, policy implementation, and judicial interpretation.

questions.text: A major feature of the United Nations system is the
options: Principle of one member, one vote in the Security Council
Veto power held by the five permanent members of the Security Council
Exclusive authority of the General Assembly over international peace
Absence of any judicial body to settle disputes
questions.explanation: The veto power of the P5 (US, UK, France, Russia, China) is a defining feature of the UN Security Council, allowing any one of them to block resolutions. The Security Council does not have one member, one vote; that is the General Assembly's principle. The Security Council has primary responsibility for peace, and the ICJ exists as a judicial body.

questions.text: The term 'political party system' refers to the
options: Internal structure of a single political party
Number of political parties in a country and their relationship
Electoral laws governing the conduct of elections
Ideological orientation of the ruling party
questions.explanation: A party system describes the configuration of parties in a country, including the number of parties (e.g., one-party, two-party, multi-party) and the nature of their interaction (e.g., competitive, dominant, or fragmented). It is not about a single party's structure, electoral laws, or ideology, though these influence the system.

questions.text: The Nigerian civil service is expected to be
options: Appointed solely based on political loyalty
Subject to periodic dissolution after elections
questions.explanation: A professional civil service is characterised by permanence, political neutrality, and anonymity (officials implement policy without taking public credit). It should not be partisan, appointed solely on political grounds, or dissolved after elections. This ensures continuity and professionalism.

questions.text: The concept of 'political stability' is essential for
options: The suppression of all civil liberties
questions.explanation: Political stability—the absence of significant political violence, unrest, or governmental change—creates a predictable environment conducive to investment, planning, and social harmony, which are essential for development. It does not imply military rule, the end of parties, or suppression of liberties.

questions.text: The African Union's Agenda 2063 is a strategic framework for
options: Creating a single African state under one central government
Achieving a peaceful, prosperous, and integrated Africa
Establishing African dominance over the global economy
Replacing the United Nations in Africa
questions.explanation: Agenda 2063 is the AU's blueprint for socio-economic transformation, aiming for a prosperous, integrated, and peaceful Africa driven by its own citizens. It does not seek to create a single state, dominate the global economy, or replace the UN. It is a vision for the continent's development.

questions.text: A major feature of the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani political system was the
options: Strong emphasis on a council of elders (Oha)
Centralised rule of the Emir with a hierarchical bureaucracy
System of direct democracy through village assemblies
questions.explanation: The Hausa-Fulani system was highly centralised under the Emir, who exercised executive, judicial, and religious authority with a hierarchical structure of officials (such as the Waziri and Galadima). The Igbo system had councils of elders and village assemblies, which were decentralised. The Hausa-Fulani system was not a direct democracy.

questions.text: The United Nations General Assembly consists of representatives from
options: Only the five permanent members of the Security Council
All member states of the United Nations
Only member states from the Global South
The member states of the European Union
questions.explanation: The General Assembly is a universal body where all 193 UN member states are represented on the basis of one state, one vote. It is not restricted to the P5, the Global South, or the EU. It is the most representative organ of the UN.

questions.text: The concept of 'foreign policy' is the
options: Domestic strategy for managing internal conflicts
Set of strategies and principles a state uses to manage its relations with other states
Legal framework for local government administration
questions.explanation: Foreign policy encompasses the goals, strategies, and actions a state takes to advance its interests in the international arena. It is distinct from domestic policy, economic programmes for poverty, or local government frameworks.

questions.text: A major challenge facing the African Union is the
options: High level of political and economic integration among member states
Lack of any conflict or crisis on the continent
Implementation of its decisions and protocols by member states
Absence of any regional economic communities
questions.explanation: A significant challenge for the AU is the gap between policy adoption and implementation at the national level. Many member states fail to ratify or domesticate AU protocols, hindering continental integration. The AU faces many conflicts, and implementation is a key problem.

questions.text: The principle of 'self-determination' is the right of
options: A state to determine its own foreign policy
A people to determine their own political status and pursue their own economic, social, and cultural development
The government to determine the laws of the land
A political party to determine its own candidate
questions.explanation: Self-determination is a principle in international law that allows a people, often defined by a shared identity, to freely decide their political status and pursue their development. It is a people's right, not a state's right, a government's right, or a party's right.
